Seattle.metaTitle: Seattle, WA Side Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Seattle.metaDescription: Seattle owners own the side sewer to the main, SDCI permits every repair, and only a Registered Side Sewer Contractor works the street. See where CIPP fits.
Seattle.article:
Why Seattle Calls It a Side Sewer

In Seattle the pipe between a building and the public main is a side sewer, and the city has a code chapter, a dedicated permit, and a licensed trade built around it. Under Seattle Municipal Code 21.16.190 the owner of the property it serves owns and maintains that pipe whether it sits in the yard, under the sidewalk, or beneath the street, all the way to, but not including, the tee or wye on the main. That framework is the first thing Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, sorts out before quoting Sewer Techs' Seattle side sewer lining: who will hold the permit, and whether the street side of the job falls under the city's registration rule.

The Registered Side Sewer Contractor Rule

Most Washington cities accept any state-licensed, bonded contractor for right-of-way work. Seattle goes further. SMC 21.16.055 says side sewer work in a public place must be performed by a Registered Side Sewer Contractor, an RSSC, with a certified person from the city roster supervising on site, and 21.16.060 sets the bond and insurance behind the registration. SDCI Tip 503 applies the rule to trenchless work: lining in the right-of-way needs an RSSC even when nothing is excavated there, and the RSSC must hold the permit. The same requirement reaches work within five feet of a public main or inside a city easement. An owner can permit the yard portion, but once the job touches the street side, the permit belongs to a registered contractor.

What the SDCI Side Sewer Permit Covers

The Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections issues the permit, and the work that needs one includes installation, alteration, repair, capping, relocation, removal, and, named specifically, pipe lining and pipe bursting. An emergency repair can start first if the application reaches SDCI by the next business day. Every pipe must be seen by an SDCI inspector before it is covered, and 21.16.140 adds a tightness test in the inspector's presence to confirm the line neither takes in groundwater nor leaks sewage. An approved as-built drawing closes the permit, and street work adds an SDOT street use permit.

Two-Thirds Combined, One Consent Decree

Seattle's older neighborhoods still carry sewage and stormwater in the same pipe. SPU's capital plan counts 968 miles of combined sewer against 448 miles of sanitary sewer, roughly two-thirds combined. In a hard rain the excess spills from outfalls into the lakes, the Ship Canal, the Duwamish, and Puget Sound. On July 3, 2013 the city entered a federal consent decree with EPA and the Department of Ecology committing to a Long Term Control Plan that brings every outfall down to the state standard of one untreated overflow per year on average. King County, which runs the regional trunks and plants, signed its own decree that year. Ecology lists 85 Seattle outfalls and 38 county outfalls, nearly 70 percent of the state's permitted CSO points, and both deadlines moved from 2030 to 2037 after the agencies asked for more time in 2019.

The Ship Canal Tunnel and the Pipe Under Your Lawn

The largest piece of that plan is the Ship Canal Water Quality Project, a 29-million-gallon tunnel beneath Ballard, Fremont, Wallingford, and Queen Anne that holds combined flow until the plants can take it. EPA backed it with a $192.2 million WIFIA loan against $561.2 million in construction cost. None of that money touches a private side sewer, yet the decree also binds the city to a maintenance program targeting no more than four sanitary sewer overflows per 100 miles of pipe, and every cracked side sewer that drinks groundwater in a storm works against it. The tightness test on repaired pipe is the city's lever on the private side; a seamless liner that passes it is one less leak feeding a tunnel built to catch rain.

Where Lining Belongs in a Seattle Side Sewer

Cured-in-place pipe suits Seattle because so many side sewers run through steep yards, under mature trees, and beneath arterials where an open cut means pavement restored to SDOT standards under 21.16.280. A resin-saturated liner is pulled or inverted from a cleanout and cured into a continuous pipe with no joints for roots to find. A side sewer that has collapsed, sheared at a joint, lost its slope, or settled into a belly cannot be lined, because the liner takes the shape of whatever it cures against. Those sections are burst or dug, and the call comes from a camera run after cleaning. If the video shows a bad connection at the main, SPU procedure DWW-340.1 lets the owner submit the footage and ask the utility to rule on whether the tee is the city's defect to fix.

Houses Older Than the Treatment Plants

The 2009-2013 American Community Survey counted 309,205 housing units, with 89,639, or 29 percent, built in 1939 or earlier and another 30,204 from the 1940s. Add the 35,868 units of the 1950s and about half the city's homes predate any secondary treatment plant on Puget Sound. Beneath them run concrete and vitrified clay side sewers laid in short sections, often shared between neighbors under the joint-use rules in 21.16.250, with cast iron under postwar basements. Clay opens at every joint and old concrete erodes from the crown down. SPU tells owners to camera the line every eight to ten years, every two to three near big trees, and always before buying. Permit records thin out with age, so the camera, not the paperwork, decides whether a line can take a liner.
faq: Who is responsible for a side sewer in Seattle, including the part under the street?

The property owner. Seattle Municipal Code 21.16.190 assigns ownership, operation, and maintenance of the side sewer to the owner of the property it serves, in public and private places alike, up to but not including the tee or wye on the public main. SPU maintains the main and that connection fitting only.
Can any licensed plumber line my side sewer in Seattle?

Not if any part of the work is in the right-of-way, within five feet of a public main, or inside a city easement. Those jobs must be done, and the permit held, by a Registered Side Sewer Contractor on Seattle's roster under SMC 21.16.055. A plumber can still camera and clean the line without a permit.
Does CIPP lining need a permit from the City of Seattle?

Yes. SDCI Tip 503 names pipe lining and pipe bursting among the work types that require a side sewer permit, alongside repair, replacement, and capping. The line must be inspected before it is covered, pass a tightness test where one applies, and be documented with an approved as-built drawing before the permit closes.
How does Seattle's combined sewer system affect a homeowner's pipe?

About 968 of Seattle's 1,416 miles of wastewater pipe carry sewage and stormwater together. The 2013 federal consent decree requires the city to control overflows at all 85 of its outfalls, now by 2037. Groundwater entering through a cracked private side sewer adds to the storm flow the city is spending hundreds of millions to store.
When should a Seattle side sewer be replaced instead of lined?

When a camera inspection after cleaning shows collapse, a sheared joint, a belly holding water, or a run that has lost its fall toward the main. A liner copies the host pipe's shape, so it cannot restore slope or bridge a missing section. Those lengths are burst or excavated; the rest of the line can often still be lined.

Tacoma.metaTitle: Tacoma, WA Side Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Tacoma.metaDescription: Tacoma separated its sewers by 1993, yet owners still own the side sewer into the street. Permits, lining rules, till, old pipe. See where CIPP fits.
Tacoma.article:
A Sewer System That Finished Separating in 1993

Tacoma's first sewers, laid in 1880, ran straight to tidewater on Commencement Bay, and for seven decades rain and sewage shared those outfalls. A 1944 bond built the first treatment plant, finished in 1952 as today's Central plant; a 1955 report told the city to split storm flow from sewage, and the last storm drain came off the sewer in 1993, which is why Tacoma, unlike Seattle or Everett, has no combined sewer overflow outfalls on the Department of Ecology's list. That history shapes how trenchless sewer repair in Tacoma is permitted and inspected. Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, is based in the city and works to that standard.

Separated Pipes Still Leak Into the Plants

Taking the storm drains off the sewer did not stop rain from getting in. Environmental Services says wet-weather flow can reach seven times normal, enough to overload the Central and North End plants, back sewage into basements, and send partially treated effluent into the bay. The inflow and infiltration program begun in 1995, at about $4 million a year, replaces leaking mains and smoke-tests for roof drains still tied to the sewer. The private half is the side sewer: groundwater seeping through broken joints is infiltration, a downspout plumbed into the line is inflow, and the Side Sewer Manual forbids either from entering the sanitary sewer.

Your Pipe Reaches the Middle of the Street

Tacoma's code defines the private side sewer as the owner's pipe from about two feet outside the building to the connection with the public system, and notes that most of that length lies under streets and alleys. The city maintains the main and the tee, wye, or riser where the side sewer joins it; everything upstream is the owner's to clear, repair, or replace, and 12.08B.530 adds that the owner rebuilds any curb, sidewalk, or pavement opened during the work. There is no property-line handoff: a root ball under the asphalt is as much the homeowner's problem as one under the porch, and the restoration bill makes digging there the costliest way to reach it.

The Permit Comes From PDS, the Rules From Environmental Services

TMC 12.08B.150 requires a city permit before anyone repairs, rehabilitates, replaces, or builds a private side sewer, and ties the work to the Side Sewer and Sanitary Sewer Availability Manual. Planning and Development Services issues it after Environmental Services review. Right-of-way work must be done by a state-licensed, bonded contractor who pulls the permit; a homeowner may permit and perform work confined to private property. A city inspector watches every job, prepares a record drawing, and tests new or repaired pipe before backfill with a ten-foot water column or an air test held at 3.5 psi. Old permit cards can be pulled through GovMe, though the city warns its files are thin for older homes.

How Tacoma Decides Whether a Liner Is Allowed

Few Washington cities write cured-in-place pipe into their standards as plainly as Tacoma. The Side Sewer Manual lists CIPP as an approved gravity material beside PVC, HDPE, and vitrified clay, then sets the conditions for accepting it. The host pipe must be televised first, with an inspector present on 24 hours' notice or by recorded video filed with the permit. The run may not sag more than a quarter of its diameter, turn more than 45 degrees at a bend, carry an offset joint over a tenth of the diameter, or be more than a quarter out of round. After curing, a second video is run with the inspector watching. Pipe bursting has its own gate: the same sag limit, no utility conflicts, and fused HDPE as the new pipe. Those numbers say what every honest installer says: a liner cannot fix a belly, a collapse, or a line that has lost its grade. That pipe is burst or dug out, and the pre-lining video is where the answer shows up.

Till, Slopes, and the Pipes Under Pre-1950 Houses

Pierce County's sewer plan maps Vashon till across northern Tacoma: dense, glacially compacted silty sand and gravel that water cannot pass easily. Winter rain moves sideways along the top of the till, so North End and West Slope yards weep for months and a clay side sewer with open joints sits in saturated ground half the year. The housing on that till is old: the city's 1995 Consolidated Plan found 52 percent of Tacoma's homes already predated 1950, and city sewer records only become reliable after that date. Concrete and clay side sewers of that vintage were laid in short sections whose joints roots in Proctor, Stadium, and Hilltop have had a century to find, while South Tacoma ranch houses carry cast iron corroding along the bottom.

Selling, Remodeling, and the Side Sewer Flyer

Tacoma tried a mandatory point-of-sale side sewer inspection in 2010 as part of its infiltration push. What survives in the code is an education rule: under 12.08B.530, real estate professionals must hand the city's side sewer flyer to buyer and seller before title transfers, and the city gives the same flyer to anyone permitting a substantial renovation, an addition, or a new building that may sit over the private line. The manual holds an addition or remodel worth 60 percent or more of the building's value to new-construction standards and requires a televised, pressure-tested line before an old side sewer can serve a new structure. A buyer who cameras the line before closing has the leverage; one who waits inherits the pipe. Qualified owners can finance repairs through the Environmental Services Conservation Loan Program; violations carry civil penalties up to $10,000 a day under 12.08B.500.
faq: Where does the City of Tacoma's responsibility for my sewer line begin?

At the public main. Tacoma maintains the main plus the tee, wye, or riser where your side sewer connects. The code defines the private side sewer as the owner's pipe from about two feet outside the building to that connection, and most of it runs under the street or alley, so the owner is responsible for the length beneath the pavement too.
Does Tacoma allow CIPP lining of a residential side sewer?

Yes, with conditions. The Side Sewer Manual lists cured-in-place pipe as an approved gravity material and requires a pre-lining video, no sag over 25 percent of the diameter, no bend over 45 degrees, no joint offset over 10 percent, and host pipe no more than 25 percent out of round, followed by a post-lining video with a city inspector present.
What permit do I need to repair a side sewer in Tacoma?

A side sewer permit under TMC 12.08B.150, issued by Planning and Development Services after Environmental Services review. Right-of-way work must be done by a state-licensed, bonded contractor who holds the permit; owners may permit work on their own property only. The pipe is inspected and tested before backfill. Clearing a clog needs no permit.
Is a side sewer inspection required when selling a house in Tacoma?

Not under the current code. TMC 12.08B.530 requires real estate professionals to give buyers and sellers the city's side sewer educational flyer before a sale closes, and the city hands the same flyer to permit applicants for substantial renovations and additions. The flyer explains that the owner alone is responsible for the private line.
Why does Tacoma care about rain getting into private side sewers if its sewers are separated?

Because storm flow still reaches the plants through cracks and illicit connections. Environmental Services reports wet-weather flows up to seven times normal in its separated system, which can cause basement backups and overflows to Commencement Bay. Its inflow and infiltration program, running since 1995, targets leaking mains, roof drains, and broken private side sewers.

Spokane.metaTitle: Spokane, WA Side Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Spokane.metaDescription: Spokane owners maintain the side sewer to the main, stub included. Permits, the no-backfill rule, CSO tanks, basalt, pre-1960 clay pipe. See where CIPP fits.
Spokane.article:
A Combined Sewer City With a River Running Through It

Spokane still moves sewage and storm runoff through the same pipes across much of town. The City's Wastewater Management division says more than 400 miles of combined sewer remain in service, concentrated on the South Side, and in a hard rain those pipes used to spill a mix of stormwater and sewage into the Spokane River at numbered outfalls along the gorge. Every private side sewer on the South Hill and in Browne's Addition feeds that network. When a homeowner here asks about cured in place pipe in Spokane, the work being quoted by Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, is a private lateral draining into a system the City has spent two decades trying to keep out of the river.

Twenty Tanks Under the Streets

The fix the City chose was storage. Rather than tear up the South Side to separate every combined line, Spokane built twenty underground concrete tanks that catch the storm surge and release it back to the Riverside Park Water Reclamation Facility once the pipes have room. The tank beneath Spokane Falls Boulevard holds 2.2 million gallons; the last of the twenty went into service in August 2020. The permit target is blunt: no more than one overflow per year at each discharge location. The tanks belong to the Integrated Clean Water Plan adopted by the City Council in May 2014, roughly $300 million in projects that also added membrane treatment at the plant for phosphorus and PCBs. That storage is finite, and clear water leaking into cracked laterals during a storm eats into it.

The Side Sewer Is Yours, Stub Included

Under SMC 13.03.0187 a side sewer is a privately maintained line that begins two feet outside the building wall and runs to the public sewer, expressly including the stretch inside the public right-of-way. The October 2025 Side Sewer Installation Handbook spells out the consequence: the owner maintains and repairs the entire side sewer to the main, and once connected, the stub between the main and the property line is the owner's problem too. SMC 13.03.0312 adds a deadline. If a blocked or broken private sewer is not corrected within two days of notice and the Wastewater Director or Health Officer finds a public health risk, the City can do the repair and bill the parcel.

Permits, Inspectors, and the Two-Day Rule

Any work on the line, whether new construction, repair, alteration, extension, or abandonment, needs a Sewer Connection Permit from Developer Services, good for twelve months. Work in the street adds a Street Obstruction Permit. The handbook requires at least one working day's notice to book a Wastewater inspector, and SMC 13.03.0624 forbids backfilling until the installation has passed; an owner who covers the trench early pays to open it again. Only Washington licensed and bonded contractors may build side sewers; owners doing their own work must first meet an inspector on site and may not touch the right-of-way.

What the City Says About Lining

Spokane's handbook addresses rehabilitation directly, which few Washington cities do. Vitrified clay or concrete pipe that is cracked but still straight may be lined or replaced by trenchless methods, and when a new foundation lands over an existing sewer, lining, slip-lining, or bursting is accepted before footings go in. Reusing an old service requires a Relay/Repair Permit and camera video proving the pipe is viable. Orangeburg and other bituminous fiber pipe cannot be reused at all, and the City's belly agreement states what every honest installer knows: lining and bursting do not fix a sag. A low spot stays a low spot under a liner, and so does a lost grade, a collapsed section, or a sheared joint. Those runs are excavated or burst, not lined.

Basalt Knobs and a Gravel Aquifer

The USGS maps Columbia River basalt exposed in knobs along Dean Street near Washington and along Perry Street near Third Avenue, and Five Mile Prairie is a basalt-capped plateau. On the lower ground the valley is filled with sand, gravel, cobbles, and boulders left by the Missoula floods, the deposits that form the Spokane Valley-Rathdrum Prairie Aquifer. EPA named it a Sole Source Aquifer in 1978, it supplies drinking water to more than 500,000 people, and near the river the water table sits less than fifty feet down. Rock makes an open trench slow and costly; gravel means a leaking lateral is losing sewage into the ground that feeds the city's wells. Both favor a liner installed from a cleanout, with no trench, when the lateral is cracked but still round.

Seventy-Year-Old Houses, Seventy-Year-Old Pipe

The City's analysis for the 2021 Housing Action Plan put the average detached house in Spokane at about seventy years old, using 2020 assessor data, and a 2016 Housing Quality Task Force briefing reported 69 percent of the city's housing built before 1960. The Hillyard, Logan, West Central, and South Hill grids are full of pre-war houses whose laterals were laid in vitrified clay with mortar or tar joints; postwar tracts added concrete and, in some years, Orangeburg. A camera run before any quote tells you which you have. If the pipe holds its shape, CIPP is usually the least disruptive answer. If not, the City's low-interest Utility Service Line Repair and Replacement loan, run through SNAP for owners at or below 80 percent of area median income, can help pay for the dig.
faq: How far does my responsibility for a Spokane side sewer go?

All the way to the public main. Spokane Municipal Code 13.03.0187 defines the side sewer as private from two feet outside the building to the public sewer, including the length under the street, and the City's Side Sewer Installation Handbook says the stub between the main and the property line becomes the owner's once it is connected.
Which permit covers a side sewer repair or liner in Spokane?

A Sewer Connection Permit from the City's Developer Services office, which covers construction, repair, alteration, extension, and abandonment and stays valid for twelve months. Work in the street adds a Street Obstruction Permit. Reusing an inactive service requires a Relay/Repair Permit plus camera video showing the pipe is sound.
Does Spokane allow trenchless lining of an old clay side sewer?

Yes, when the clay or concrete pipe is cracked but still straight. The City handbook names lining, slip-lining, and pipe bursting as acceptable ways to deal with such pipe. It also states that these methods do not correct bellies, and Orangeburg pipe may not be reused under any method.
What do Spokane's CSO tanks have to do with my lateral?

Most of the South Side still drains sewage and stormwater through shared pipes. The City built twenty underground tanks, finished in 2020, to hold storm flows and keep overflows to one per year per location. Groundwater leaking into cracked private laterals during storms uses up that storage, which is why a sealed lateral matters here.
Is there help paying for a side sewer repair in Spokane?

The City's Utility Service Line Repair and Replacement Program, run through SNAP, offers low-interest loans repaid on the monthly utility bill to owners in the City's service area with household income at or below 80 percent of area median. It covers crushed, broken, or leaking side sewer pipe, permits, excavation, and related street or sidewalk restoration.

side_sewer_definition.value: SMC 13.03.0187 defines a side sewer as a privately maintained sewer, not controlled or maintained by a public authority, beginning two feet outside the building's outer wall or foundation and carrying wastewater from the building drain to a public or private sewer, including portions within the public right-of-way.

owner_responsibility.value: The City's Side Sewer Installation Handbook (October 2025) states that the property owner is responsible for maintenance and repair of the entire side sewer, including the portion in the public right-of-way, and that the side sewer stub between the main and the property line becomes the owner's responsibility after connection.

permit_and_inspection.value: A Sewer Connection Permit (valid 12 months) is required to connect, construct, repair, alter, extend, or abandon a sewer; inspections need at least one working day's notice; SMC 13.03.0624 requires that the trench not be backfilled until the installation passes inspection, with the owner or contractor paying for any re-excavation. Side sewers must be built by Washington licensed and bonded contractors; owners may do their own work only with Director approval and never in the right-of-way.

prompt_repair_rule.value: SMC 13.03.0312 (ORD C36776, effective Jan. 18, 2026) makes the owner, customer, or occupant responsible for fixing a blocked or broken private sewer; if not corrected within two days of notice and the Health Officer or Wastewater Director finds a public health risk, the City may repair it and charge the owner.

Vancouver.metaTitle: Vancouver, WA Sewer Lateral Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Vancouver.metaDescription: City sewer or Clark Regional Wastewater District? Who owns the lateral under VMC 14.04.100, the trenchless repair permit, river plants. See where CIPP fits.
Vancouver.article:
Which Utility Owns the Main Under Your Street

The City of Vancouver's wastewater utility runs about 791 miles of pipe and 48 pump stations and, as of mid-2023, served close to 244,000 people across 58.6 square miles, inside and outside the city limits. Clark Regional Wastewater District, a separate special-purpose district, serves about 100,000 people from Hazel Dell and Felida out to Orchards and Ridgefield, and it owns mains on some blocks inside city limits. Each issues its own permits. Before scheduling Sewer Techs' Vancouver side sewer lining, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer will want to know which agency's main your lateral taps, because that decides who inspects the work.

The Lateral Belongs to the Customer, Street and All

For City customers the rule is written into Vancouver Municipal Code 14.04.100. Subsection G makes the customer responsible for installing, owning, and maintaining the sewer lateral from the premises to the public main at their own cost, which puts the segment under the sidewalk and roadway on the homeowner. The City carves out one narrow exception: if a lateral inside dedicated right-of-way is damaged by the City's own crews or its contractors, the owner can file an itemized claim within ten days and be reimbursed up to the cost of a new lateral from the main to the property line. Root damage from the owner's trees, storms, and the owner's contractors are excluded, so in practice the City pays for very few lateral repairs.

A Permit Written for Trenchless Work

Vancouver stands apart from most Washington cities in having a permit built around lining and bursting rather than open trenches. The City's Trenchless Service Lateral Repair Permit, backed by a January 2024 requirements document, governs relining, bursting, or directional drilling of a lateral inside public right-of-way or a sewer easement in the City's service area. The contractor files a narrative and a diagram showing the method, pipe material, DR rating, diameter, cure method, pit locations and dimensions, the length of work inside the right-of-way, and a bypass pumping plan. Engineering staff aim to review a complete package in two business days before the Right-of-Way Permit issues. The on-lot portion is permitted separately as plumbing work through the Building Department, and VMC 14.04.100(I) requires a licensed contractor as the owner's agent for everything in the street.

What the City Checks on a Finished Liner

The requirements read like a punch list for a CIPP crew. The cured liner may not protrude into the public main, and no annular gap may remain between the liner and the host pipe. No new cleanout may be added inside the right-of-way, and the liner may not introduce any change of direction or slope there. When the job is done, Construction Services expects a video showing the full lined length within the right-of-way through to the main connection, and the repair must pass its testing and inspection before the permit closes. In District territory the track is different: a District side sewer permit, with the trench left open until a District inspector approves it.

When the Pipe Cannot Be Lined

Vancouver's trenchless rules say nothing about bellies or sags, and that silence is not permission. A liner takes the shape of whatever it is installed in. A lateral that has dropped into a low spot where water stands, lost its grade, split open and let soil in, or telescoped at a joint will produce a liner with those same defects, and the City's video will show them. Those pipes are candidates for pipe bursting, which pulls a new pipe through the old alignment, or for an open-cut replacement permitted the ordinary way. Cracks, root intrusion at joints, light offsets, and corroded cast iron under a slab are where a camera inspection usually confirms lining is the right tool.

Two Plants on the Columbia

Everything a Vancouver lateral carries ends up in the Columbia River. The City treats its flow at two facilities: the Marine Park plant east of downtown, opened alongside the Water Resources Education Center in 1996 on a bond package of about $40 million, which releases treated water near the Renaissance Trail, and the Westside plant, whose discharge permit, WA0024350, Ecology circulated for renewal in spring 2026 with an outfall at river marker 105.1. Forty-eight pump stations lift flow from the low ground along the river to gravity mains, and every gallon of groundwater that seeps into a broken lateral is pumped and treated alongside sewage. Near the river and in Fruit Valley the water table is shallow enough that a cracked clay lateral can run half full of clean water all winter.

Houses From the Shipyard Boom

Vancouver's housing has a sharp age divide. The Hough neighborhood northwest of downtown holds the city's largest surviving collection of pre-World War II houses, built roughly 1890 to 1945 and listed on the Washington Heritage Register in 2003; Arnada and Carter Park are similar. Then came the war. The National Park Service records that Kaiser's shipyard drew about 38,000 workers to the riverfront, the city's population roughly doubled to around 50,000 between 1940 and 1948, and the Vancouver Housing Authority built some 12,000 units, including the thousand-acre McLoughlin Heights east of the old city. Much of that wartime and early postwar housing is still occupied, on laterals of clay, concrete, and sometimes Orangeburg laid in a hurry. East of I-205 the stock is newer; the state counted 85,511 housing units citywide in 2022, up 21 percent in a decade. The old core is where the lining calls come from.
faq: Does the City of Vancouver or Clark Regional Wastewater District serve my house?

It depends on who owns the main in your street, not on your mailing address. The City's service area extends beyond the city limits, and the District owns mains on some blocks inside the city. Your utility bill names the agency. The City's trenchless lateral rules apply only where the City owns the main.
Who is responsible for a broken sewer lateral in Vancouver, Washington?

The customer. VMC 14.04.100(G) assigns installation, ownership, and maintenance of the lateral from the building to the public main to the property owner, including the part under the street. The City reimburses right-of-way repairs only when its own crews or contractors caused the damage, and only on a claim filed within ten days.
What permit does a CIPP lateral liner need in Vancouver?

Inside the public right-of-way or a sewer easement, a Right-of-Way Permit issued under the City's Trenchless Service Lateral Repair Permit process, which requires a narrative, a diagram of the method and pit locations, and a bypass plan reviewed by Engineering Services. The on-lot portion needs a plumbing permit from the Building Department.
What does Vancouver inspect after a lateral is lined?

Construction Services requires a post-construction video covering the entire liner within the right-of-way and its connection to the main. The liner may not stick into the main or leave an annular gap, no new cleanout may be placed in the right-of-way, and no new change in direction or slope is allowed.
Which Vancouver neighborhoods have the oldest sewer laterals?

The pre-war core: Hough, listed on the Washington Heritage Register with houses from about 1890 to 1945, plus Arnada, Carter Park, and the blocks around Esther Short. The World War II shipyard boom added thousands of units such as McLoughlin Heights. Laterals of that era are typically clay or concrete, with some Orangeburg.

Bellevue.metaTitle: Bellevue, WA Side Sewer Stubs, Permits & CIPP Lining
Bellevue.metaDescription: Bellevue owns the side sewer stub under the street; you own the rest. BCC 24.04.115, the side sewer permit, 1960s-70s pipe, lake lines. See where CIPP fits.
Bellevue.article:
The Stub Belongs to the City, the Run Belongs to You

Bellevue draws its sewer boundary where most Washington cities do not. Under Bellevue City Code 24.04.115 the utility owns every sewer facility in public right-of-way or an accepted easement, and the code names side sewer stubs among them: the stretch of your side sewer between the public main and the right-of-way or easement line. Everything on the house side of that line is private, and the same section makes the owner responsible for maintaining and repairing it along with its cleanouts, check valves, and pumps. In most of the region the owner is on the hook all the way to the main, pavement included, so a Bellevue homeowner researching cured in place pipe in Bellevue starts with a smaller problem than a neighbor in Seattle or Kirkland. Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, lines the private run; the stub under the asphalt is Bellevue Utilities' asset.

What the Boundary Means When a Camera Finds a Defect

The value of 24.04.115 shows up on inspection day. A crushed section or root ball under the planting strip or the travel lane is city pipe; Bellevue describes the utility maintaining mains and service connections inside right-of-way and dedicated easements, and it counts more than 120 miles of lateral pipe tying mainlines to customer side sewers. A defect under your lawn, driveway, or slab is yours. The city will not locate pipe on private property, though staff will share the as-built drawings they have, with the caveat that they must be field verified.

The Side Sewer Permit and the Inspector's Hold on Backfill

Any new side sewer, and any addition, repair, or connection to an existing one, needs a side sewer permit under BCC 24.04.120, filed through MyBuildingPermit by the owner or by a licensed, bonded contractor who is also registered with Bellevue's tax office. Permits run two years. Bellevue Utilities' permit conditions are blunt about sequencing: nothing gets backfilled until the utilities inspector has looked at it, tested it, and signed off, and pipe covered early is dug back up at no cost to the city. A repair permit cannot include right-of-way work; touching the stub or the street needs a separate Right of Way permit and crushed-rock backfill with a compaction report. A lining job inside the property line needs the side sewer permit, a call to 811, and an inspection that reviews the post-cure video instead of an open trench.

Where the Flow Goes: Renton, by Way of 34 Connections

Bellevue has never run its own treatment plant. Its roughly 520 miles of mains and 13,000-plus maintenance holes deliver wastewater to 34 major connections with King County's Wastewater Treatment Division, and from there to the South Treatment Plant in Renton, operating since 1965 and averaging about 90 million gallons a day from Bellevue, Kent, Auburn, Renton, Issaquah, and Sammamish. King County's charge is the largest item on a Bellevue sewer bill, and it tracks volume. Groundwater seeping into a cracked private side sewer in a November storm is water Bellevue pays the county to treat.

Infiltration Was Worse Than the Models Assumed

Bellevue's Wastewater System Plan leans on a 2002 King County infiltration study, and on the city's follow-up work, which found far more rainwater and groundwater entering the pipes than earlier planning had assumed. The plan warns that unchecked inflow and infiltration eats downstream capacity, raises overflow risk, and drives capital spending, and it calls for targeted reduction. The lake lines are the most visible symptom: about 15 miles of pipe along the Lake Washington shoreline and 4 more in Lake Sammamish, built in the late 1950s and 1960s, flat enough to need daily flushing, with the oldest asbestos-cement segments in Meydenbauer Bay dating to about 1952. Those lines have their own replacement program. The private side sewers draining toward them do not.

Postwar Ranches on Glacial Ground

Of Bellevue's roughly 61,000 housing units, only about 2 percent predate 1950; 11 percent went up in the 1950s and 39 percent in the 1960s and 1970s. Those two boom decades produced the ramblers and split-levels of Lake Hills, Newport Hills, Eastgate, and Crossroads, built as the sewer district pushed mains into former farmland. Their side sewers are concrete or vitrified clay in short joints, often with cast iron for the first few feet out of the foundation, bedded in glacial till that holds water all winter. Fifty to sixty years on, the joints have opened, roots from mature firs and maples have followed the moisture in, and the cast iron has scaled and channeled. The pipe usually still holds round, which is the fact that matters most for what comes next.

When Lining Is Right in Bellevue, and When It Is Not

Cured-in-place lining suits the typical Bellevue failure: an intact clay or concrete side sewer with leaking joints, roots, and scattered cracks between the house and the right-of-way line. The resin-saturated liner goes in through a cleanout, is pressed against the host pipe, and cures into a continuous wall with no joints for roots or groundwater to find, and no trench through a landscaped yard or a concrete driveway. Lining is the wrong answer for pipe that has lost its shape. A collapsed section, a joint sheared by settlement, a belly holding standing water, or a run that has lost its slope cannot be corrected by a liner that simply follows the host; those defects call for pipe bursting or open-cut replacement under the permit rules above. A recorded pre-lining camera survey is what separates the two.
faq: Does the City of Bellevue own any part of my side sewer?

Yes. Bellevue City Code 24.04.115 puts the side sewer stub, the portion in the public right-of-way or an accepted utility easement between the main and the property line, under city ownership. The side sewer from that line to your building is private, and you are responsible for maintaining and repairing it along with its cleanouts and any check valve or pump.
Is a permit needed to line a sewer pipe on private property in Bellevue?

Yes. BCC 24.04.120 requires a side sewer permit for any repair, addition, or connection to an existing side sewer, applied for through MyBuildingPermit by the owner or a licensed, bonded contractor registered with the city. The work is inspected by Bellevue Utilities, and a repair permit cannot include right-of-way work, which needs its own permit.
Who do I call when sewage backs up in a Bellevue house?

If sewage is rising inside while no water is being used, call Bellevue Utilities Wastewater Operations at 425-452-7840; crews respond around the clock. If only one drain is slow or the backup follows a shower or laundry load, the city treats it as a private side sewer problem and expects you to bring in a plumber or a camera inspection first.
Where does Bellevue's sewage actually get treated?

Not in Bellevue. The city's mains feed 34 connections to King County's regional system, and the flow is treated at the South Treatment Plant in Renton, which has operated since 1965 and handles about 90 million gallons a day. King County's treatment charge is the largest piece of a Bellevue sewer bill and is tied to the volume the city sends.
Why are 1960s and 1970s Bellevue homes the most common lining candidates?

Because 39 percent of the city's housing was built in those two decades, on sewer mains extended through former farmland, with clay or concrete side sewers in short jointed sections and cast iron near the foundation. After five or six decades the joints leak and roots follow, but the pipe usually still holds its shape, which is the condition a liner needs. Collapsed or bellied pipe must be replaced instead.

Everett.metaTitle: Everett, WA Side Sewers, CSO Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Everett.metaDescription: North Everett still runs on combined sewers built 1890-1963. Side sewer ownership (EMC 14.08.260), backwater valves, the 2027 CSO deadline. Where CIPP fits.
Everett.article:
A City Split Between Two Kinds of Sewer

Everett's sewer map has a seam in it. The north end runs on combined pipes that carry roof runoff, street drainage, and sewage together, most laid between 1890 and 1963, starting with clay pipe down Broadway in 1890. South Everett came later on separated sewers. On a combined block a December storm fills the main to the crown and pushes back toward every connected basement; a separated main sees only what the houses send. Which side of the seam a home sits on is the first thing Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, checks before quoting Sewer Techs' Everett side sewer lining, because it decides whether a liner alone solves the problem or a backwater valve has to go in beside it.

Thirteen Outfalls and a 2027 Deadline

When the combined system overfills, the surplus leaves through 13 outfalls into the Snohomish River and Port Gardner Bay. Everett has been cutting those discharges since its 1987 CSO Control Plan and reports annual overflow volume down more than 95 percent. The current push is governed by Ecology Agreed Order 11638, which allows no more than one overflow per outfall per year by the end of 2027. The centerpiece is the Port Gardner Storage Facility, a roughly $200 million conversion of the former Kimberly-Clark industrial treatment plant into wet-weather storage for four bayside outfalls, due to be operating by December 31, 2027. On the river side, a 1.8-million-gallon tank under 36th Street will hold excess flow from two basins. All of it is about keeping rainwater out of sanitary flow, which a sealed private side sewer does at a smaller scale.

The Right-of-Way Line Is the Line

Everett Municipal Code 14.08.260 settles ownership cleanly: once a side sewer connection is installed and approved, the sewer department owns and maintains the part inside the public right-of-way and takes no responsibility for the part outside it. EMC 14.08.270 assigns each abutting owner the side sewer from the premises to the right-of-way. The code also scripts a blockage: the owner pays to investigate first, with a cable machine or camera, to show which side of the line the stoppage is on; if it points to the street, the city investigates and the public works director decides. When the cause is a broken service line in the right-of-way, the sewer fund reimburses the owner's last drain-cleaning bill, so keep the invoice. Ignore an order to fix a broken private drain for two days and the city may do the work and lien the property.

Permits Are Cheap; Skipping Them Is Not

Under EMC 14.08.060 no one may open, alter, or repair a sewer tied into the municipal system without a permit, and 14.08.140 prices it: $30 for repairs to an existing side sewer, $60 plus $10 for a new connection, and nothing for root cutting through an existing cleanout. Permits run 180 days. Section 14.08.160 puts all permitted work under city inspection and acceptance, and a licensed sewer contractor who refuses an inspector's correction forfeits the license. Public Works now handles this work as Site Work permits. A liner is a repair to an existing side sewer and carries the $30 permit; digging that reaches the street needs separate right-of-way approval.

Backwater Valves and the Surcharge Rule

Everett wrote its basement-flooding experience into EMC 14.08.180 in 2014. The department can designate at-risk connections in the combined area and mail owners a deadline, at least six months out, to install an approved backwater prevention device; new connections with fixtures below the upstream manhole rim need one regardless. The leverage is in the claims rules: past the deadline, a designated property without a working valve collects nothing from the city for a storm backup, and no owner can recover for damage a disconnected downspout would have prevented. A rebate program helps with the valve. The liner enters at a cleanout and the valve sits at the house outlet, so doing both in one mobilization avoids opening the same pit twice.

Bluffs, Fill, and a Pre-1950 Housing Stock

North Everett sits on a peninsula of glacial sediment that drops steeply to the bay on the west and the Snohomish River lowlands on the east. The city publishes landslide and erosion hazard maps and treats drainage as what moves those slopes; a side sewer leaking into a bluff feeds the groundwater that lubricates a slide. The housing on top is old: the 2024 housing element counts about 15 percent of Everett's 43,800 units as built before 1940 and another 12 percent from the 1940s and 1950s, and an earlier element put the pre-1950 share at 23 percent against 9 percent countywide. Those Riverside, Bayside, Northwest, and Delta houses have clay side sewers with mortar or tar joints, often running to alley mains, under foundations that have shifted for a century. Roots, offsets, and infiltration are the norm, and on a combined block each opening lets surcharged sewage back toward the basement.

Where Lining Earns Its Place in Everett

A cured-in-place liner is a good match for a century-old clay side sewer that still holds its circle: the resin tube is inverted or pulled from a cleanout, cured against the host, and leaves a seamless pipe roots and groundwater cannot re-enter, without trenching a 1910 foundation, a brick retaining wall, or a steep lot where an excavator cannot sit. It is not a cure for geometry. A sag that pools water, a joint sheared by bluff creep, a collapsed barrel, or a run that has lost its fall will fail the same way after lining, because the liner takes the shape it is given; those need pipe bursting or replacement. The camera recording made before any quote tells an Everett owner which repair they are buying.
faq: Who owns the side sewer under the street in Everett?

The city. Everett Municipal Code 14.08.260 gives the sewer department ownership and maintenance of approved side sewer connections inside the public right-of-way, and no responsibility beyond it. Under EMC 14.08.270 the abutting owner maintains everything from the building to the right-of-way line, which in older north Everett neighborhoods often runs to an alley rather than the street.
If my Everett sewer backs up, who pays the drain cleaner?

You do, at first. The code requires the owner to investigate with a cable machine or camera to show which side of the right-of-way line the blockage is on. If it turns out to be a broken city service line in the street, the city sewer fund reimburses your last drain-cleaning invoice. If the problem is on your property, the repair and the bill stay with you.
What permit does a sewer lining job need in Everett?

EMC 14.08.140 lists a $30 permit for repairs or alterations to an existing side sewer, which is how a liner is classified; cleaning and root cutting through a cleanout need none. Permits last 180 days, must be posted on site, and the work is inspected and accepted by Public Works. Any digging that reaches the street requires separate right-of-way approval from the city engineer.
Why does Everett push backwater valves in north Everett?

Because the north end still runs on combined sewers built between 1890 and 1963 that surcharge in heavy rain. EMC 14.08.180 lets the city designate at-risk connections and set an installation deadline; after that date, a designated property without a working valve cannot collect from the city for a backup. A rebate program helps with the cost, and downspouts must stay off the combined sewer.
What is the Port Gardner Storage Facility and why does it matter to homeowners?

It is a roughly $200 million conversion of the old Kimberly-Clark industrial treatment plant into wet-weather storage for four of Everett's 13 combined sewer outfalls, required by Ecology Agreed Order 11638 to be running by December 31, 2027. It exists to keep stormwater-swollen flow out of the bay, the same reason a leaking private side sewer in the combined area is worth sealing.

Kent.metaTitle: Kent, WA Side Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Kent.metaDescription: Three sewer agencies serve Kent, each with its own lateral ownership rule and permit desk. Valley alluvium vs. hill till, 1960s housing. See where CIPP fits.
Kent.article:
One Kent Address, Three Possible Sewer Utilities

In Kent, the agency that owns the pipe under your street depends on which hill you live on. The valley floor and much of both hills are served by the City of Kent's own sewer utility. A long stretch of the East Hill plateau, including territory annexed around Panther Lake, is inside Soos Creek Water and Sewer District, a district founded in 1939 that lists Kent among the six cities it serves. A slice of the West Hill falls inside Midway Sewer District, which treats its own flow at the Des Moines Creek plant on Puget Sound. Before anyone quotes trenchless sewer repair in Kent, read your utility bill and learn which of the three you pay, because the ownership line and the permit desk change with the answer. Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, works in all three.

The Side Stub Is Yours in Kent, Not in Soos Creek

Kent City Code 7.04.040(B) puts the entire side sewer on the owner: once the city approves a connection, the owner and every later owner must maintain, repair, unclog and operate the line, and that duty runs through the right-of-way to the public main, tee and side stub included. Accepting the connection creates no duty on the city. Soos Creek draws the line differently. It describes a connection as a stub from the main to the property line plus a side sewer from the stub to the house, and it maintains the main and the stub while the customer maintains the side sewer. A Soos Creek customer with a backup calls the district first so a crew can say which side the fault is on; a City of Kent customer owns the same problem out to the middle of the street.

Pulling a Sewer Permit at 400 West Gowe

KCC 7.04.050 requires a permit for any work that builds, extends, relays or repairs a building sewer or side sewer, on private ground or in the right-of-way. Applications go through the Permit Center at 400 W. Gowe Street with a scaled site plan showing the full side sewer route. The contractor must hold a Washington contractor registration under RCW 18.27 and a Kent business license. The applicant must call for inspection before any underground work is covered, street work adds a separate Street Use Permit, permits expire after six months, and starting without one doubles the base fee. Soos Creek issues its own Repair Permit with the as-built drawing.

Everything Drains Toward Renton

Kent and Soos Creek flows both end at King County's South Treatment Plant on Monster Road in Renton, running since 1965 and treating about 90 million gallons a day. King County bills the local agencies, not homeowners, and that regional arrangement is why it cares about private laterals. Its Infiltration and Inflow program estimates that clear water leaking into sanitary pipes makes up roughly three-quarters of winter peak flow and names aging side sewers on private property as the main contributor. Every open joint in a Kent lateral is a small storm drain feeding a plant built for sewage, and sealing it is the one I&I fix a homeowner can order directly.

Valley Floor Alluvium Versus Hill Till

The valley floor is Green River floodplain, flat and water-logged, the saturated low ground King County's hazard plan ranks as most prone to liquefaction. Soos Creek's hazard annex reports about 40 percent of its sewer service area and 19 of its lift stations in mapped liquefaction zones. Pipes laid in that material settle unevenly, which is how a lateral develops a belly, a low spot that holds water and solids. Up on the hills the ground is glacial till, firmer but cut by ravines where KCC 11.06.375 flags slopes of 40 percent or more with ten feet of relief as landslide hazard areas. Hill laterals tend to crack and offset at joints rather than sag, and the two failure modes call for different repairs.

What a Liner Can and Cannot Do Under a Kent Lot

Cured-in-place pipe installs a resin-wetted tube through an existing cleanout, presses it against the host pipe, and hardens it into a jointless new wall. Sewer Techs installs Perma-Liner and Easy Liner systems sized for the four- and six-inch laterals Kent's standards call for, usually without opening the driveway or street. The method has hard limits. A valley lateral with a real belly cannot be lined; the liner follows the sag and the low spot stays. A pipe that has collapsed, sheared at a joint, or lost its grade needs pipe bursting or an open trench. Cracked, root-bound or corroded pipe that still holds its round shape is the right candidate, and only a recorded camera run from house to main tells which you have. Estimates are free. Call now at (877) 811-9027.

Houses From the Boeing Boom and the Panther Lake Annexation

Kent's housing element reports that more than 40 percent of the city's homes were already over 30 years old when it counted 41,481 units in 2012, about 5,000 of them added by the Panther Lake annexation. The ranch houses and split-levels that filled the hills during the 1960s and 1970s aerospace expansion are now past 50, and King County notes that a side sewer is usually the same age as the house above it and may be clay, concrete, iron or plastic. Concrete and clay of that era separate at joints under root pressure; cast iron under slabs thins along the bottom. Both commonly stay round enough to line, which is why a camera-verified liner is often the least disruptive fix for a Kent owner.
faq: Who owns the sewer pipe under the street in front of my Kent house?

If the City of Kent is your sewer utility, you do. Kent City Code 7.04.040(B) makes the owner responsible for the whole side sewer out to the public main, including the tee and side stub inside the right-of-way. If Soos Creek Water and Sewer District serves you, the district maintains the stub from the main to the property line and you maintain the rest.
How do I know whether Kent, Soos Creek or Midway is my sewer provider?

Look at who bills you for sewer. The City of Kent utility covers the valley and much of both hills, Soos Creek Water and Sewer District covers parts of the East Hill plateau and the Panther Lake area, and Midway Sewer District covers a portion of the West Hill. The three have separate permit desks, so confirm before scheduling any lateral work.
What permit does a side sewer repair or lining job need in Kent?

In the city's service area, KCC 7.04.050 requires a sewer permit for repairing or relaying a side sewer, pulled at the Permit Center at 400 W. Gowe with a scaled site plan. The contractor needs state registration and a Kent business license, inspection must happen before anything is covered, and street work adds a Street Use Permit. Soos Creek issues its own Repair Permit.
Why does King County care about my private sewer lateral in Kent?

Because Kent's wastewater goes to the county's South Treatment Plant in Renton, and the county estimates that groundwater and stormwater leaking into sanitary pipes make up about 75 percent of winter peak flow, mostly through aging private side sewers. A sealed lateral keeps clear water out of a regional plant that treats roughly 90 million gallons a day.
Can a sewer line in the Kent valley be lined if it has a low spot?

Usually not. Valley-floor laterals sit in soft Green River alluvium that settles, and a liner installed through a belly simply hardens in the same sagging shape, so solids keep collecting there. A bellied or collapsed section has to be burst or dug and regraded. Cracked or root-damaged pipe that still holds its shape is a good lining candidate; a camera inspection settles it.

Olympia.metaTitle: Olympia, WA Side Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Olympia.metaDescription: LOTT treats it, Olympia owns the mains, and a right-of-way cleanout decides who owns your lateral. Downtown fill, 1900s houses. See where CIPP fits.
Olympia.article:
Four Partners, One Plant on Budd Inlet

Olympia built its first treatment plant on the Budd Inlet waterfront in 1952. Tumwater bought in by contract in 1955, Lacey tied in during 1969, and in 1976 the three cities and Thurston County signed the interlocal agreement that produced the acronym LOTT, made a standalone nonprofit in 2000. LOTT owns the Budd Inlet Treatment Plant, which handles about 12 million gallons a day and has removed nitrogen since 1994, plus 18 miles of interceptors under Plum Street, Capitol Boulevard and Martin Way. Everything smaller, from the collector in your street to the pipe at your foundation, is City of Olympia or private property, which matters when a homeowner is weighing Sewer Techs' Olympia side sewer lining: LOTT never touches a lateral, and the rules come from Olympia Municipal Code. Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, knows them well.

The Cleanout Decides Who Owns the Pipe

Olympia moved its ownership line in 2016, with a condition attached. Under OMC 13.08.040(B), a gravity side sewer that has a cleanout at the right-of-way or easement line belongs to the owner only from the house to that cleanout; the city owns the run from the cleanout to the main. Without that cleanout the owner owns the whole pipe to the main, as every Olympia owner did before 2016, and the owner must install and keep up the boundary cleanout so city crews can reach it. One clause cuts against the grain: 13.08.040(C) says that whoever owns the pipe, the owner clears any blockage between house and main if the cause began on private property, roots, grease or broken pipe included.

Permits, Taps and the 48-Hour Rule

OMC 13.08.030 forbids opening or connecting any sewer without a permit from Community Planning and Development. The Engineering Design and Development Standards, Section 7B.080, add a sewer lateral permit before any connection, six-inch minimum pipe from the main to the right-of-way line, a cleanout at the boundary and at every 100 feet or 90-degree turn, and a city inspector notified two working days ahead to witness any tap. New laterals are jetted and televised from the boundary cleanout to the main, with no standing water anywhere in the run. Street work requires a licensed contractor bonded to the City Engineer's satisfaction under 13.08.080. The same standards require trenchless rehabilitation of an existing side sewer to follow ASTM F1216, the cured-in-place specification, so lining is an anticipated repair, not an exotic one.

Downtown Sits on 1911 Dredge Spoil

Much of the downtown peninsula is not original ground. The 1910-1911 dredging campaign pulled roughly two million tons of mud out of Budd Inlet to create new waterfront blocks and bury the Swantown Slough that once separated the Eastside from downtown. That low 450-acre district now holds the Port and LOTT's plant, and the city's 2019 Sea Level Rise Response Plan, written jointly with LOTT and the Port, plans for 24 inches of rise by 2050 and 68 by 2100. Downtown still runs a combined storm and sewer system that strains in big storms, and the plan warns that six inches of rise could push flooding into it and overwhelm the plant. Fill also shakes badly, as the 1949, 1965 and 2001 earthquakes showed. For a lateral in that soil, settlement and offset joints are the expected defects.

Concrete, Clay and 1,800 STEP Tanks

The city's Wastewater Management Plan counts about 187 miles of gravity sewer and 31 lift stations. By length, 47 percent of the gravity pipe is PVC, 41 percent is concrete and 9 percent is vitrified clay, with traces of asbestos cement and cast iron. PVC only became standard in the mid-1970s, so that concrete and clay half is the older network, and private laterals nearby are usually the same vintage. Olympia also runs roughly 1,800 septic tank effluent pumping systems and 280 private grinder pumps on flat, low ground, and about 4,225 septic systems remain in the city and its growth area; OMC 13.08.020 requires connection once a main is within 200 feet.

Where CIPP Earns Its Place in Olympia

A cured-in-place liner is a resin-saturated tube inverted or pulled through the lateral from a cleanout, inflated against the host pipe, and cured into a smooth, jointless wall. For an Olympia owner the appeal is practical: no trench across a 1920s sidewalk in South Capitol, no street cut that triggers the bonding rules, and a sealed pipe that stops admitting the groundwater OMC 13.08.150 forbids sending to the sanitary system. Sewer Techs lines with Perma-Liner and Easy Liner materials and verifies each job by camera. Lining is a gravity-pipe repair; pressurized STEP and grinder lines are a different trade. A lateral that has collapsed, dropped into a belly, or lost its slope cannot be lined, because the liner would freeze the defect in place; those runs need pipe bursting or excavation. Estimates are free, so call now: (877) 811-9027.

Streetcar Suburbs and Postwar Blocks

Olympia's oldest neighborhoods predate its sewer plant by half a century. The city's historic preservation plan dates South Capitol's houses mostly to 1900 through 1928, with one from 1878; Bigelow Highlands grew as a working-class district after 1900; the Eastside filled in once electric streetcars ran in 1892; and the West Side developed after 1880. Those houses were plumbed with cast iron inside and clay outside, and their laterals have absorbed a century of roots, settlement and three major earthquakes. The postwar ring around the 1952 plant added concrete laterals under houses now past 70. Both generations commonly remain round enough to line, so a camera inspection, not the age of the house, should decide between a liner and a trench.
faq: Does LOTT Clean Water Alliance fix sewer laterals in Olympia?

No. LOTT owns the Budd Inlet Treatment Plant, 18 miles of interceptors and three major pump stations, and it bills through the partner cities. The collector mains in Olympia streets are City of Olympia property, and the side sewer from your house is governed by Olympia Municipal Code 13.08, so lateral questions, permits and repairs go through the city, not LOTT.
Who owns the side sewer under the street in Olympia?

It depends on whether a cleanout exists at the right-of-way or easement line. If it does, OMC 13.08.040(B) gives the city the segment from the cleanout to the main and leaves the owner the run from the house to the cleanout. If there is no boundary cleanout, the owner owns the entire pipe to the main until one is installed.
Do I need a permit to line a sewer lateral in Olympia?

Yes. OMC 13.08.030 requires a permit from Community Planning and Development before opening or connecting to any sewer, and the city's engineering standards require a sewer lateral permit, boundary cleanouts, and CCTV video of the finished line. Those standards specifically require trenchless side sewer rehabilitation to follow ASTM F1216, the cured-in-place pipe standard.
Why is downtown Olympia a special case for sewer pipes?

Downtown sits on roughly 450 acres of fill, much of it dredged from Budd Inlet in 1910 and 1911, served by a combined storm and sanitary system. The 2019 Sea Level Rise Response Plan projects 24 inches of rise by 2050 and warns that six inches could flood that system and the LOTT plant. Fill settles and shakes, so offset joints and sags are common lateral defects there.
Can my Olympia STEP system or grinder pump line be lined with CIPP?

Generally no. Cured-in-place lining is a repair for gravity pipe that still holds its shape. The pressurized small-diameter lines from a septic tank effluent pump or grinder pump, which the owner maintains under OMC 13.08.040, are replaced rather than lined. Gravity laterals from the house to a STEP tank or to a city main are candidates once a camera confirms they are not collapsed or bellied.

Bremerton.metaTitle: Bremerton, WA Sewer Lateral Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Bremerton.metaDescription: Bremerton owns the sewer lateral to your property line; you own the rest. Permits, the five-day repair rule, beach sewers, wartime homes. See where CIPP fits.
Bremerton.article:
Bremerton Draws Its Ownership Line at the Property Line

Most Washington cities hand the homeowner the whole pipe out to the main. Bremerton does not. Under Bremerton Municipal Code 15.03.090, the connection from the wastewater main to the property line belongs to the City, stays under its exclusive control, and is maintained by Public Works. The engineering standards repeat it: City to the property line, owner from there to the structure. That split changes what a camera inspection means here. A defect between the property-line cleanout and the main is Bremerton's problem. A defect between the cleanout and the house is yours, and that is the stretch where Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, offers Sewer Techs' Bremerton side sewer lining as an alternative to digging up the yard.

Twenty Years and Fifty Million Dollars of Overflow Work

Bremerton's older neighborhoods were sewered like most pre-1945 Puget Sound towns: one pipe for sewage and rain, with relief outfalls to the water. The City counts fifteen designated combined sewer overflow outfalls. Planning began in 1989, Ecology approved the first CSO Reduction Plan in 1992, and by 2009 every outfall met the state limit of one overflow a year; Ecology closed out the plan in February 2011. The bill came to roughly $50 million across 23 projects, including 12.5 miles of new pipe, 275,000 gallons of storage, and a new Eastside treatment plant. Overflow volume fell by more than 99 percent, and the state reopened Dyes Inlet shellfish beds in 2003 citing that progress. A $450,000 cooperative program also disconnected residents' downspouts and driveway drains from the sewer.

Sewer Mains Buried Under the Beach

The strangest feature of Bremerton's system is how much of it was laid along the shoreline. Mains run under beaches along the Narrows and the bays, where tides make them hard to reach, grit washes in, and sewage sits one break from salt water. Since 2014 the City has been retiring those lines: 12,500 feet so far in Manette, along Washington Avenue, at Pump Station CW-4, and in Oyster Bay, with 9,600 feet more planned and Ostrich Bay next, a program priced near $28 million. Homes that drained downhill to a beach main are re-plumbed uphill with a small pump; the City pays installation and the owner pays a monthly maintenance charge. Over 200 such pumps are running, and the standards forbid new connections to any remaining beach sewer.

What the Permit Office Expects

The City's wastewater standards require a permit, held by the property owner, to connect, cap, or repair a side sewer, good for 180 days. The contractor gives 24 hours' notice, and nothing may be covered until the inspector approves it; work buried early is dug back up at the owner's expense. City crews video repaired laterals before acceptance. The design rules are specific: four-inch minimum residential side sewer, two percent slope, cleanouts at the property line and within five feet of the building, and a backwater valve wherever grades or a pressure main create backflow risk under BMC 15.03.120. Pressure side sewers and grinder pump work require a Washington-licensed contractor.

Five Days, Then the Water Goes Off

Bremerton's code is blunt about private pipe that has failed. BMC 15.03.170 gives an owner five days from notice to repair a side sewer that is obstructed, broken, or failing; miss it and the Director may shut off water to the property. Two other provisions push toward replacement. When a house is rebuilt on the same lot, BMC 15.03.200 requires the old side sewer to be videoed and approved before reuse, with anything substandard replaced. When an owner reactivates a dormant lateral, the City videos it free, and an inadequate one must be replaced with new six-inch pipe or, where feasible, reconditioned by trenchless methods. In other words, the City's own standards accept trenchless rehabilitation as a code-compliant fix.

Shipyard Houses on Shipyard Hills

Bremerton grew up around the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard, and the Second World War built much of its housing in a rush. Population jumped from about 15,000 to 72,500 during the war, and the draft housing appendix to the 2044 Comprehensive Plan reports that nearly 36 percent of occupied homes predate 1950, with another 23 percent from the 1960s and 1970s. Sinclair Park alone added 280 houses above Sinclair Inlet in 1943 and was gone by 1948. What survives sits on steep ground above the Narrows and the inlets, with clay or concrete side sewers and, under the house, cast iron that has spent seventy or eighty years corroding from within. The Manette conversion shows the terrain: shoreline lots now pump up to the main on Wheaton Way.

Choosing Between a Liner and a Trench in Bremerton

Cured-in-place lining threads a resin-saturated tube through the side sewer from a cleanout, inflates it against the old wall, and cures it into a seamless pipe that bridges open joints, root holes, and eaten-away invert. The City trusts the method enough to spend about $700,000 a year lining its own mains against infiltration. On a terraced Bremerton lot that means no trench down the slope and no rebuilt retaining wall. It is not always the right call. A side sewer that has collapsed, telescoped at a joint, sagged into a standing belly, or lost its slope on a creeping hillside cannot be lined, because the liner would copy the failure; those runs need pipe bursting or open excavation. A camera inspection settles it before anyone quotes a price. Estimates are free. Call now: (877) 811-9027.
faq: Who fixes a broken sewer lateral under the street in Bremerton?

The City does. Bremerton Municipal Code 15.03.090 places ownership of the connection from the wastewater main to the property line with the City, and Public Works maintains that segment. The property owner is responsible only for the side sewer from the property-line cleanout to the building, which is the portion a private contractor would line or replace.
Does Bremerton require a permit to line or repair a side sewer?

Yes. The City's wastewater engineering standards require a permit, in the owner's name, to connect, cap, or repair a side sewer. The contractor must give 24 hours' notice, nothing can be backfilled until inspected, and the permit lapses after 180 days. Pressure side sewers and grinder pump work must be performed by a Washington-licensed contractor.
What happens if I ignore a City notice about my failed side sewer?

Under BMC 15.03.170 you have five days from notice to repair a side sewer that is obstructed, broken, or failing. If the work is not done, the Director may terminate water service to the property until it is. Owners sharing a private sewer are jointly liable for any work the City has to perform.
Why is Bremerton removing sewer mains from its beaches?

Older mains were laid under the shoreline, where tides make them difficult to maintain, grit enters the system, and a break discharges straight to the water. Since 2014 the City has retired about 12,500 feet in Manette, along Washington Avenue, and in Oyster Bay, with roughly 9,600 feet more planned, moving affected homes to small pumps that push uphill to street mains.
Can a hillside Bremerton home have its sewer lined instead of dug up?

Often, yes. If the camera shows the pipe still holds its round shape and slope, a cured-in-place liner can be installed from a cleanout without trenching down the slope. If the hillside has shifted the pipe, broken it, or created a belly where water stands, lining will not correct it and the run must be burst or replaced.
