Bellingham.metaTitle: Bellingham, WA Side Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining Guide
Bellingham.metaDescription: Bellingham's side sewer is yours all the way to the main, street included. Permits, smoke tests, Post Point, Lake Whatcom dig season. See where CIPP fits.
Bellingham.article:
Yours All the Way to the Main

Bellingham Municipal Code 15.12.060(E) makes the property owner responsible for the entire service connection, including the portion inside the public right-of-way, up to where it joins the City main, and adds that the City is not liable for damage from blockage or deterioration anywhere along that run. Public Works says the same on its sewer page: the owner maintains the side service, tap included, and the City does not repair it. With more than 19,000 side services on roughly 300 miles of mains, that is a lot of private pipe under public streets. That is why Sewer Techs, the Washington CIPP Verified Installer, treats CIPP lining for Bellingham side sewers as a street-to-house job: the liner can run the full length, through the right-of-way, without opening the pavement.

What Happens When You Report a Backup

Public Works takes backup calls around the clock, and the response follows a fixed logic. A crew checks the main on either side of your connection; if it flows freely upstream and downstream, the stoppage is judged to be in the side service and the owner is called to arrange the repair. There is no shared-cost program and no exception for the stretch under the sidewalk. Owners also hear from the City in quieter moments: crews running cameras or smoke through a main note side services with roots or holes and tell the owner. That notice is the cue for your own camera inspection before the first winter backup.

The Water/Sewer Permit and the Inspector's Visit

Bellingham's Development Guidelines and Improvement Standards require a Water/Sewer Permit to connect, repair, or modify any connection to the City sewer, issued by Public Works through the Permit Center either with a building permit or as a General Public Works Permit, after connection and inspection fees are paid. Section 15.12.060 adds the field rules: a state-licensed contractor makes the connection, materials come from the City's accepted list, and nothing is covered until Public Works has inspected it. Opening the street adds an obstruction bond. Bellingham keeps no registered side sewer contractor roster the way Seattle does, but a lining job that reaches the main still goes through the same permit and inspection.

Smoke in the Lettered Streets

Bellingham's sewers date to 1892, when one network carried sewage and rain straight to Whatcom Creek and the bay. The systems were separated over the following decades, but the oldest neighborhoods still send rainwater into the sanitary side through cracked laterals and drains that were never disconnected. When flow meters show the sewers swelling during storms, Public Works runs an inflow and infiltration investigation: smoke testing on G Street and the West North Street area of the Lettered Streets and Cornwall Park neighborhoods was a recent pilot. The City has also tried the direct route. In one neighborhood program it replaced private side sewers with new four-inch pipe at its own cost, disconnected the roof and yard drains it found, and handed the finished pipe back under a signed agreement that maintenance from house to main was the owner's from that day on.

Post Point and the Bay at the End of the Pipe

Everything the side sewers collect ends up at the Post Point Resource Recovery Plant on McKenzie Avenue. Primary treatment began in 1947 near the mouth of Whatcom Creek; Post Point replaced that plant in 1974, sized for a 55-million-gallon-a-day peak. A $55 million upgrade brought secondary treatment in 1993, and a capacity expansion finished in 2014. Treated water leaves through an outfall roughly a quarter mile out in Bellingham Bay at a depth of 60 feet. Behind it run about 318 miles of gravity sewer, 6 miles of pressure main, and 29 lift stations, and a new Comprehensive Sewer Plan begun in 2026 and due in 2028 will size the next round of investment. Groundwater leaking into a Lettered Streets lateral rides all the way there and takes up room built for sewage.

Digging Inside the Lake Whatcom Watershed

Part of the city drains to Lake Whatcom, the drinking water source for more than 100,000 people, and the rules there change how a sewer repair gets done. Ground-disturbing work in the watershed, meaning clearing, grading, filling, or exposing soil, is allowed only from June 1 through September 30, and bare soil must be covered by October 1. The City's standards drop the land disturbance permit threshold there to 120 square feet, which a single trench crosses quickly. A lateral that fails in January cannot wait for summer; a liner installed through an existing cleanout disturbs almost no soil, which is the practical way around that calendar when the pipe qualifies.

Houses From 1900 and the Pipe Beneath Them

Bellingham's historic districts tell you where the oldest laterals are. Fairhaven's core dates from about 1890 to the First World War, the Lettered Streets filled in around 1900, York was built out before the Depression, and South Hill's working-class houses went up as the century opened. The 2016 Comprehensive Plan counts more than half the city's housing as built before 1980 and nearly a third as more than fifty years old. Under those houses the side sewers are vitrified clay or concrete in short lengths, a joint every few feet for roots to find, running through glacial soils to mains often as old. Cured-in-place lining suits that pipe when the camera shows it still round and sloping: a resin-saturated tube is inverted from the cleanout, cured hard, and the joints disappear. It does not suit pipe that has collapsed, separated, or bellied, which must be burst or replaced. Estimates are free. Call now: (877) 811-9027.
faq: Does the City of Bellingham maintain any part of my sewer lateral?

No. BMC 15.12.060(E) places the entire service connection, including the part under the street or in a utility easement, on the property owner, up to the connection with the City main. Public Works will check that the main is flowing when you report a backup, but repairing the side service, wherever the defect sits, is the owner's job.
What permit covers a side sewer repair or lining job in Bellingham?

A Water/Sewer Permit from Public Works, obtained through the Permit Center, is required to connect, repair, or modify any connection to the City sewer. The work must be done by a state-licensed contractor, use City-accepted materials, and stay uncovered until a Public Works inspector approves it. Work in the street may also require a street obstruction bond.
Why is Bellingham smoke testing sewers in older neighborhoods?

Flow monitoring showed sewer flows rising during rain, so Public Works ran an inflow and infiltration pilot in the Lettered Streets and Cornwall Park neighborhoods. Smoke blown into the main escapes wherever rainwater can get in, revealing cracked laterals and connected roof or yard drains. The goal is to keep clean water out of Post Point.
Can I dig up a sewer line on a Lake Whatcom watershed lot in winter?

Watershed rules limit clearing, grading, and soil exposure to June 1 through September 30, and Bellingham's land disturbance permit threshold inside the watershed is only 120 square feet. A winter emergency should go through the Permit Center first. Lining through an existing cleanout avoids most of that disturbance and is often the workable option.
Where does Bellingham's wastewater go after it leaves my house?

To the Post Point Resource Recovery Plant on McKenzie Avenue, which replaced the 1947 Whatcom Creek plant in 1974, gained secondary treatment in 1993, and was expanded in 2014. Treated effluent is discharged through an outfall about a quarter mile into Bellingham Bay at 60 feet of depth.

A third-party listing describes a City side sewer repair loan (up to $15,000 at 3%, repaid on the utility bill); I could not confirm it on cob.org, so it is omitted. Bellingham has no registered side sewer contractor program that I could find; the article says so and relies on the state-license requirement in 15.12.060(C).
